title: The Melt
principle: Why invest: inflation catch-up and saving for retirement
product: Savings account, Fixed Deposit, real vs nominal returns

lessons.title: Meet The Melt
lessons.subtitle: The same money buys less over time
lessons.capability: Explain inflation with an everyday example.

steps.speaker: melt
lines: Hehehe. I'm The Melt. Every year, I make your money buy a little less.
You can't stop me. But maybe… you can outgrow me.

steps.speaker: kip
lines: The Melt is inflation: prices slowly rising over time.
Let's see what it does to a cup of chai.

steps.title: The chai test
steps.caption: Drag the years. Watch the price climb and your ₹1,000 shrink.

predict.question: A chai costs ₹20 today. With 6% inflation every year, what will it cost in 20 years?
predict.reveal: About ₹64. At 6%, prices roughly double every 12 years, and the rise itself compounds.

steps.brief: Coins in your pocket are idle money. The Melt shrinks them when it gets close. Steer into green INVEST gates to bank them!

steps.question: What does inflation do to money kept in a drawer?

options.why: The notes are still there! They just buy less each year.

options.text: Same number of rupees, but they buy less
options.why: Exactly. The number stays the same; its buying power shrinks.

options.text: Nothing, if you don't spend it
options.why: The Melt works even on money you don't touch. That's the sneaky part.

steps.title: Inflation in India
steps.realLife: The RBI aims to keep consumer inflation around 4%, within a 2–6% band. Even 4% a year halves your money's buying power in about 18 years.
steps.deeper: India measures inflation with the Consumer Price Index (CPI), published every month by the government's statistics office. Your personal inflation can differ: college fees and phones can rise faster than the average.

lessons.title: Why prices rise
lessons.subtitle: Demand, costs and too much money

steps.speaker: dash
lines: My favourite samosa went from ₹15 to ₹20! Is the shopkeeper scamming me?

steps.speaker: kip
lines: Probably not! Prices rise for a few big reasons. Tap each one.

items.title: More demand than supply
items.text: Festive season: everyone wants sweets at once, so prices go up.

items.title: Costs go up
items.text: When fuel, potatoes or rent cost more, the shopkeeper passes it on.

items.title: Too much money
items.text: When lots of money chases the same goods, each rupee buys less.

items.title: The RBI's job
items.text: The RBI raises interest rates to cool inflation and lowers them to support growth.

steps.question: Potato and oil prices jump. What usually happens to samosa prices?

options.text: They go up, because costs went up
options.why: Right. When ingredients cost more, prices follow. That's cost-push inflation.
Higher costs rarely make prices fall. The shop would lose money.
Shops can absorb costs for a while, but eventually prices rise.

steps.question: Inflation is running too hot. What can the RBI do?

options.why: That usually makes inflation worse! More money chasing the same goods pushes prices up.
Yes. Higher rates make borrowing costlier, so spending slows and price rises cool down.
Price bans cause shortages. Central banks use interest rates instead.

steps.title: Inflation on the news
steps.realLife: The RBI's Monetary Policy Committee meets regularly to set the repo rate, its key interest rate. When the news mentions inflation, it usually means CPI: the price of a basket of everyday things.
steps.deeper: When the RBI changes the repo rate, banks usually adjust loan and FD rates over the following weeks. That's why the FD rate you see today can differ from last year's.

steps.speaker: kip
lines: Here's a sneaky trick money plays on us.
A bank might pay you 3% interest. Sounds like growth, right?

steps.title: Real value after 10 years
steps.caption: Tap a product. Compare its rate with The Melt.

predict.question: A savings account pays 3%. Inflation is 6%. After 10 years, your ₹10,000 buys…
predict.reveal: Less! About ₹7,500 worth of today's stuff. Your balance grew, but The Melt grew faster.

options.why: Inflation works against you, so you subtract it, not add it.
That's the nominal return: the number on your statement, not your real buying power.
Yes. Real return ≈ nominal return − inflation.

steps.question: An FD pays 7%. Inflation is 6%. What's the real return, roughly?

options.why: Right. 7% − 6% ≈ 1%. Barely ahead of The Melt, and that's before tax.
That's the nominal return. Subtract inflation to get the real one.
You added inflation. It eats returns, so subtract it.

steps.title: Card unlocked: Savings Account
steps.realLife: Banks pay roughly 2.5–4% on savings. That's great for an emergency fund you can use anytime, but it usually loses to inflation over the long run.
steps.deeper: Savings interest is taxable income. Income from a minor's investments is usually added to a parent's income for tax ('clubbing'), so plan this together with your parents.

lessons.title: Fixed Deposits: the first shield
lessons.subtitle: Lock it, earn more
lessons.capability: Explain when an FD makes sense.

steps.speaker: dash
lines: What if I lock my money away so I can't spend it? Then The Melt can't get it, right?

steps.speaker: kip
lines: Locking stops you spending it. But The Melt still works on locked money.
A Fixed Deposit pays you more interest for locking money with a bank for a while.

steps.title: Compare the shields
steps.caption: Tap Savings, then FD. Which one keeps up with The Melt?

steps.question: What usually happens if you break an FD early?

options.why: Your money is safe. You just earn a bit less.

options.text: You pay a small penalty and earn less interest
options.why: Right. Banks usually cut the interest rate slightly as a penalty.
Most banks charge a small penalty for breaking an FD early.

steps.question: Why is a bank FD considered safe?

options.text: Its value goes up every day
options.why: An FD's rate is fixed. Its safety comes from the fixed rate and insurance.

options.text: Fixed rate, and DICGC insures deposits up to ₹5 lakh per bank
options.why: Yes. DICGC insures up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, covering principal and interest.
The insurance has a limit: ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank.

steps.title: Card: Fixed Deposit
steps.realLife: Bank FDs last from 7 days to 10 years. They suit goals 1–3 years away, like a laptop. After tax they often only just beat inflation, so long goals need something stronger (World 2!).
steps.mission: Ask a parent what FD rate their bank offers today.
steps.deeper: FD interest is taxed at your income-tax slab, and banks deduct TDS above a yearly limit. Tax-saver FDs lock money for 5 years.

lessons.title: Boss: Future You needs a pension
lessons.subtitle: Inflation over a lifetime
lessons.capability: Explain why retirement savings must beat inflation.

steps.speaker: kip
lines: Big question. One day, Future You will stop working, maybe at 60.
You might live 25 more years after that. Who pays for chai then?

predict.question: What will a ₹20 chai cost when you're 60 (45 years at 6%)?
predict.reveal: About ₹275! Prices rise about 14× in 45 years. Retirement money must grow faster than The Melt.

steps.brief: Boss run! Longer and faster. Bank at every INVEST gate to outrun The Melt.

steps.question: Why start saving for retirement while you're young?

options.text: Money has more years to grow and beat inflation
options.why: Yes. Time is the biggest weapon against The Melt.

options.text: Because interest rates are higher for teens
options.why: Rates are the same for everyone. Your advantage is time.

options.text: It doesn't matter when you start
options.why: It matters a lot. You'll see just how much in Snowball Valley.

steps.question: You keep ₹1 lakh in cash for 24 years at 6% inflation. Roughly what does it buy at the end?

options.why: The Melt never sleeps. Cash loses buying power every year.
That's after about 12 years. After 24, The Melt halves it again.
Right. It halves about every 12 years: ₹1 lakh → ₹50k → ₹25k.

steps.title: World 1 complete!
steps.realLife: Retirement products in India include the NPS and EPF (for salaried workers). You'll explore them in World 9. For now, remember: idle money shrinks.
